props.title: Pulp
props.initialSlug: A blackmailed writer's pulp fiction turns deadly real

sections.content: Pulp (1972) stands as Mike Hodges' sardonic follow-up to his breakthrough Get Carter (1971), trading gritty realism for meta-noir playfulness. Michael Caine stars as Mickey King, a pulp fiction writer caught in a labyrinthine plot that deliberately mirrors the trashy novels he churns out. The film's self-aware approach to noir tropes predates similar postmodern takes like The Long Goodbye (1973) and Chinatown (1974), though with a distinctly British sensibility and dry humor.

sections.content: What makes Pulp fascinating is how it deconstructs noir conventions while simultaneously embracing them. The Mediterranean setting provides a sun-bleached contrast to traditional noir shadows, yet the plot's convolutions - involving a retired Hollywood star, mysterious assassins, and political intrigue - feel pulled straight from Raymond Chandler. The film's meta-commentary on pulp fiction writing, complete with Caine's sardonic voiceover describing events in purple prose, anticipated similar literary noir deconstructions like The Big Fix (1978) and The Late Show (1977).

Director Mike Hodges infuses the film with a deadpan absurdity that sets it apart from contemporary neo-noirs like Night Moves (1975) or Farewell, My Lovely (1975). Mickey King's adventures play out like one of his own cheap paperbacks, with Caine's deliberately wooden performance emphasizing the artificiality. The film's critique of fascism, embodied by Mickey Rooney's Preston Gilbert character, adds unexpected political depth beneath the playful surface. SUBHEAD: Legacy and Influence

sections.content: While not as celebrated as Get Carter, Pulp's self-referential approach to genre influenced later postmodern noirs like The Big Lebowski (1998) and Inherent Vice (2014). Its combination of hardboiled detective tropes with comedy anticipated films like Dead Men Don't Wear Plaid (1982) and Who Framed Roger Rabbit (1988), which similarly played with noir conventions for comedic effect.
